comments.text:
Most of the reviewers I've seen simply pander to the "Outrage mob" of those whom think a GPU is somehow "obsolete" unless it receives a leap in rasterization performance comparable to that of the RTX 4090 vs. the absurdly overpriced $2000.00 RTX 3090.. So what you're seeing now largely is this rather bizarre since of  "entitlement" by those whom insist that they should "get more for paying less".

These "reviewers" also fall miserably at informing the consumer when it comes to the "ideal resolution / settings" of these GPU's and thus the impact of "VRAM" but instead simply "set their hair on fire" and insist the GPU is somehow "crap" because some poorly optimized AAA ports struggle to run well on lower / mid -tier GPU's at resolutions / settings that aren't reasonable for the particular GPU to begin with.. 

Nobody is suggesting that "criticism" is never warranted (VRAM can / is an issue is certain instances) just that a BALANCED / RATIONAL perspective is largely lacking. This doesn't do the consumer any good and just warps reality to an unhealthy degree. You can see this in any comment section regarding this topic, 9 out of 10 commenters are simply regurgitating the largely unwarranted "outrage" of the bandwagon jumping reviewers they listen to. 

Also many reviewers are simply "jumping on the bandwagon" of the outrange mob - easy to do seeing as the economy in general is crap (see: record inflation, etc.) and pretty much ignoring all the advanced and valuable new feature sets such as AV-1, DLSS, frame generation, power efficiency, etc. The "Group Think" mentality is simply distorting reality to such a degree that the average consumer has no idea what to think other than perhaps 'Nvidia Bad" nothing else to see here. 

Nobody is saying "No criticism" is warranted simply that the hysterical / over the top commentary regarding these new RTX 4000 series GPU's is WAY OVERBLOWN. Also, much more attention should be paid to SHIT PC Ports that scale horribly with lower / mid-tier GPU's especially when it comes to VRAM. But you know, it's MUCH easier to just ride the OUTRAGE Bandwagon and say it's ALL Nvidia's fault vs. doing a RATIONAL analysis of the BIG PICTURE.

It is important to have an understanding of the performance tier of the GPU you are buying so that your expectations are reasonable. One would think people would understand that if you pay just a fraction of the price of a top-tier GPU "compromises" will need to be made from time to time but sadly this often doesn't appear to be the case. 

With that said don't get it twisted, nobody is saying people should be "super excited" about these GPU's only that reasonable expectations should be had here and the "outrage" has been way of the top because it's simply easier to pander vs. doing a thorough / thoughtful review of the BIG PICTURE

4090: 24GB, AD102 cut down by 5-10%, $1500

4070ti: 16GB, AD103 cut down by 2-5%, $700

RTX 4050 is for 1080p60fps at highest settings
RTX 4060 is for 1080p120fps at highest settings

RTX 4090 is for 4k60fps at high settings, but highest texture

Super variants might have targeted 60fps to 90fps and 120 fps to 165fps.

PC isn't similar to console for console is focus solely on gaming and easily optimized developers.

comments.text:
I have a 3070 and while I understand that 8 GB of VRAM is just enough nowadays, the examples that I see here are not very likely used in real life. Firstly, I bet most people with an NVidia Card will use DLSS Quality most of the time. The ULTRA preset is just dumb as even HU pointed out in a video some time ago comparing High vs Ultra and also often provide Optimized settings videos (good examples from them: RDR2 and Odyssey optimization guides). RT is also something that many people even with higher tier cards and enough VRAM still don't use bc of the cost in performance. Hence, the regular user is probably aiming for 1440p-DLSS Quality or 4K-DLSS Balanced (which looks better than 1440p native in my opinion)  / High (not Ultra) settings / RT OFF and when you play like that all the VRAM issues go away unless you installed some Ultra HD TEXTURES PACK as those available for Far Cry 6 and Halo Infinite.
In my own testing: neither Halo Infinite nor Far Cry 6 have VRAM issues when played at maxed out settings but WITHOUT HD TEXTURES. Same for The Last of Us 1440p or 4K Balanced High settings and so on. On the other hand, with 8Gb you depend on developers having to deliver good medium-high texture quality and well implemented streaming pools in order to make the most out of those 6Gb and 8Gb cards in contrast to 16 GB of VRAM that can eat a ton of waste before becoming a problem.
As a final note: I do support the take that companies should not be selling 8Gb cards unless targeted for low end 1080p only gaming which NVidia is trying to do with this 4060 ti at $400 in a world where 1440p is becoming the new 1080p: same world where the 3070 exists and performs better at that resolution. Hopefully the message is passed on so that consumers can vote with their wallets.

comments.text:
@smeezekitty  it’s true there are a lot of poorly optimized games out there. 

But the notion that 8gb vram should be enough for 1080p gaming because it was enough in the past is a incorrect argument.

A lot has changed between now and then. Minimum specs for hardware in the console is 16gb (10gb for series s)

Games are being developed with consoles in mind. There are technologies that make the game look better that weren’t readily available back then. UE5 for instance is capable of loading a billion triangles to make the game assets look more detailed from afar and close. This takes vram. This is just one technology among many others. 

While I’m sure there are outliers but the average 1080p game back then do not look as good use 1080p games now. This takes vram usage though. Game devs can target for more vram usage thanks to the consoles. It’s nvidia and partly AMD that’s holding PC gaming back.

I understand nvidia’s position to some extent. They’re pivoting to be an AI company. In that market vram are a premium. There isn’t that much to differentiate a ai gpu from a gaming gpu apart from the vram. Giving more vram to their gaming cards may cannabilize ai hardware sales. I bought the 3060 for instance because it was one of the cheaper cards with the most vram besides the 3090. Performance of the card wasn’t on the top of my shopping list but rather the vram and cost. It may not train ai algorithms quickly but running algorithms isn’t too difficult. This is what nvidia is afraid of. They got high on their market segmentation strategy. As the market leader, they have little interest to change the status quo despite their customer’s protest.

comments.text:
​ @TheRealWalterHWhite  Comparing current PC technologies to something as old as a PS3 makes no sense, I'm sorry. You honestly just sound like you're in denial. 

Firstly, games on PS3 & XB360 looked VERY MUCH worse than games on PC at the time. A lot of it was hidden by playing on a TV instead of a high Res monitor. The PC ports of console games at the time looked abysmal. That wasn't optimisation, it was just flat out lower quality.

Secondly, developers have been using a lot of visual tricks and work arounds to stay within very restrictive memory requirements for years. These methods can only get you so far. They worked to keep things running ok on the previous generation of consoles (albeit often only at 30fps), but they were already butting up against limits because PS4 & XBONE were already underpowered when they released. Now there's a new console gen, people expect graphical advancement, and the old memory limits on consoles, which also often dictates where PC gaming goes, have been lifted. Developers rightly want to be able to take advantage of that, and to give better graphics at higher (than last gen) frame rates, more memory is absolutely needed. SO many developers are saying this! It's not the GPU companies.

The GPU companies WANT to sell you the same outdated VRAM package for the same or greater price. YOU should want more, because that's what technological progress and mass production do ...they give you improvements every generation at a steady price point (or at least they did until Nvidia started pretending they could just dictate any price they like).

I've been building PCs and gaming since 1993. This is what the tech industry does ....it iterates ....it improves ...it moves forward. Often rapidly. When I got a 400MB hard drive, back in 1994 I thought it was enormous and I could never fill it up. Now 4TB is common. My first PC had 4MB of RAM ..that was huge at the time. Now I have 32GB. get the idea?

Thinking that the industry should sit still because can't afford to upgrade or you don't want to is just unrealistic. I get it. I don't have much money either. But saying we can stay on 8GB VRAM when we've been on it for so long already is just silly.

This is the way.

I don't actually want nVidia and AMD to manufacture e-waste.  I want 1080ti's and their contemporaries to remain relevant as long as possible and stay out of landfill.  (They're still more powerful than a PS5 afterall.)

But could you imagine the backlash if nVidia didn't launch anything below a 4090?

There's also a lot of hate being thrown at nVidia for prices that aren't exactly all their fault.  Inflation is here.  AMD has indicated they can't price cut below the 4060ti.  Samsung gave them good wafer prices that TSMC won't, and the wafer prices did translate directly to RRP last gen, enabling scalpers to come along.  It's clear that silicon isn't gonna get any cheaper moving forward as well, so find your performance needs and buy those.

And since I'm going to be called a shill anyway -- going to Samsung last gen was good for the industry and good for the chip shortage.  If nVidia stuck with TSMC, the 30 series would have had far worse availability due to supply constraints.

comments.text:
In 2019 AMD launched the 5700 XT at 400$, armed with 8GB of GDDR6 and aimed at 1080p and 1440p gaming. At the time it was good value because most games didn't require the full 8GB of VRAM that it offered, and in terms of rasterization performance it matched up well against the 2070 Super which cost 25% more. 
Nvidia launching effectively a newer equivalent  to the 5700 XT (not in performance, but in VRAM capacity + type, price and target resolution) 4 years later is a major disappointment. Any 8GB card today simply can't play some of today's AAA games at max settings, even at 1080p with RT disabled. As such, a card like this should now be categorized as the equivalent to the GTX 16-series during the period of the 20-series. Because 4 or 5 years ago, those were the cards with which you couldn't play AAA games at 1080p high/ultra settings, and they were around 200$ in case of the 1660, or lower (in the case of the 1650 or 1650 Super). Now we're paying twice as much for a card that's equivalent in performance in today's games versus those cards in 2018's games. Terrible value and a waste of everyone's time.

Totally worth it.

But that'd not be to the happiness of a CEO facing a doom prospects after Crypto madness looking at the prospects of grim numbers.

Never had much hope in RTX 40s cos I know corporates too well.

Also it is a new smaller chip with a new frontier to conquer and a new architecture... ... 

So a shop was promoting RTX 4070 to me claiming it works better or as good as RTX 3080 by also a steep discount... ... Didn't take it.

If the game makers are going to go full blast, it will be at least 24gb of Vram for the coming 'tons of textures', 'tons of points', tons of logical expressions... ... virtual like real graphics frame hitting... ... You can't expect 8gb Vram to gradually move to 12 or 16gb anymore. It is a new smaller chip, the frontier is very deeply different, exponential burst, it is like when floppy disk met CD... ... when you got this sort of technology new frontier... ...

Seriously, is 16gb Vram even enough for Unreal Engine games??? So real... ... the hair on the mole of a skin with varied up and down, pores, and sure in motion... ... only 16gb Vram? Unreal Engine can deliver more! Much more at max settings in games... ...

What a lot of people don’t get here is that the 80 series and 70 series cards have traditionally been the same GPU, just a cut down version in the 70 series. With Nvidias 4000 series, they decided that the 4080 is its own GPU (AD103 die), and the 4070 Ti (AD104 die) is a separate one. The 104 dies usually went to the 60 models while the 106 dies (which is in the 4060 Ti) usually went to the entry level GPUs (like the 3050). So after the RTX 4080, all the cards below it were moved down a performance tier (because they had a lower tier chip) but kept the same name and pricing so Nvidia can maximize margins. This is all evident in Steves data. 

The fact that Nvidia decided to make a 16GB version last minute (as evidenced by the graphics on the video cards boxes), and charged a ridiculous $500 for it, just goes to show how they’re trying to extract as much money as possible from their customers. 

Hopefully AMD is smart enough to capitalize on this, release comparable models at much lower prices.

I know I’m not buying Nvidia anytime soon for the scummy ways.

comments.text:
@DrearierSpider1  So why do you need resources at all for your system when you are playing a game? That's the point , you really don't . Having it stutter a little while closing a game , while it loads all the system resources from the hard drive is not that big of an issue when you think about it. It is absolutely possible to load up all of the 16Gb Vram by a single game on a console in theory if you really wanted to, although the absolute majority - 99% of devs ofcourse won't be bothered doing it. We are only talking about the potential here.

Also what preliminary results seem to suggest with RE remake and Hogwarts Legacy is that when it's a tad bit unoptimized then you need a 16Gb Vram buffer to have no issues with the game, but with later patches they tend to optimize it and 14Gb or perhaps 12Gb might be enough...
